newsitem.title: USA: US Army's top enlisted man faces new sex charges.
newsitem.headline: US Army's top enlisted man faces new sex charges.

text.p: The Army's highest-ranking enlisted soldier will face new charges of sexual misconduct involving a fifth alleged victim, the Army said on Friday.
Unlike previous charges, these involve an officer.

Sergeant Major of the Army Gene McKinney, already charged with 18 counts involving four service women, now has been charged with assault on an officer and solicitation of adultery with her, the Army said in a statement.
McKinney's civilian lawyer told Reuters the new charges stem from an incident between McKinney and a superior officer that was resolved in 1994.
"They're bogus. They're the weakest charges preferred yet," defence lawyer Charles Gittins said. "She was his commander, and she's a victim? I don't think so."
The case against McKinney, a popular and charismatic chief advocate for the Army's soldiers, is the latest in a series of troubling sexual incidents that have rocked the Army.
The Army is conducting a preliminary hearing to determine if McKinney will be court-martialed.

In that hearing, alleged victims have portrayed McKinney as a man who relentlessly pursued sex even after several rejections, using his powerful post as a threat against their careers. One woman said she finally gave in and had unwanted sex with McKinney while she was nearly eight months pregnant.
McKinney, 46, and a 29-year Army veteran, has denied all the charges.

In another development, McKinney's original accuser, retired Sgt. Maj. Brenda Hoster, agreed to testify after receiving assurances the defence would be restricted in questioning her about her own sex life.
Hoster last month declared she would not testify after other women who have accused McKinney of harassment were subjected to aggressive questioning from the defence.
In earlier sessions of the hearing there was "a generally abusive atmosphere in which the defence was walking over these victims," Hoster's lawyer, Susan Barnes, told Reuters.
Hoster has been assured by prosecutors and the presiding officer's legal adviser that rules to protect witnesses from "abusive questions" will be enforced, Barnes said.

Gittins has said Hoster's sexual past may be relevant only because it may affect her credibility. Another soldier has given a sworn statement saying she witnessed Hoster making love with another woman in Army barracks, which would be a violation of military law. Barnes claims the statement is false.
Hoster was the first to come forward with allegations against McKinney, leading to charges from two other Army women and a woman sailor.
